cases.sentence: Княгиня Бетси, не дождавшись конца ___, уехала из театра.
cases.explain: «последнего акта» — the genitive here marks possession, absence, or quantity.
cases.translation: Princess Betsy drove home from the theater, without waiting for the end of the last act. She had only just time to go into her dressing-room, sprinkle her long, pale face with powder, rub it, set her dress to rights, and order tea in the big drawing-room, when one after another carriages drove up to her huge house in Bolshaia Morskaia. Her guests stepped out at the wide entrance, and the stout porter, who used to read the newspapers in the mornings behind the glass door, to the edification of the passersby, noiselessly opened the immense door, letting the visitors pass by him into the house.

cases.sentence: Гости выходили на широкий подъезд, и ___, читающий по утрам, для назидания прохожих, за стеклянною дверью газеты, беззвучно отворял эту огромную дверь, пропуская мимо себя приезжавших.
cases.explain: «тучный швейцар» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.

cases.sentence: – Расскажите нам что-нибудь забавное, но не злое, – сказала жена посланника, ___ изящного разговора, называемого по-английски small-talk, обратясь к дипломату, тоже не знавшему, что теперь начать.
cases.explain: «великая мастерица» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: “Do tell me something amusing but not spiteful,” said the ambassador’s wife, a great proficient in the art of that elegant conversation called by the English small talk. She addressed the attaché, who was at a loss now what to begin upon.

cases.sentence: Я часто думаю, что ___ прошлого века были бы теперь в затруднении говорить умно.
cases.explain: «знаменитые говоруны» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: “They say that that’s a difficult task, that nothing’s amusing that isn’t spiteful,” he began with a smile. “But I’ll try. Get me a subject. It all lies in the subject. If a subject’s given me, it’s easy to spin something round it. I often think that the celebrated talkers of the last century would have found it difficult to talk cleverly now. Everything clever is so stale. …”

cases.sentence: Муж княгини Бетси, добродушный толстяк, ___ гравюр, узнав, что у жены гости, зашел пред клубом в гостиную.
cases.explain: «страстный собиратель» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: The husband of Princess Betsy, a good-natured fat man, an ardent collector of engravings, hearing that his wife had visitors, came into the drawing-room before going to his club. Stepping noiselessly over the thick rugs, he went up to Princess Myakaya.

cases.sentence: Неслышно, по ___, он подошел к княгине Мягкой.
cases.explain: «мягкому ковру» — after the preposition «по», the dative marks the indirect object or recipient.
cases.translation: The husband of Princess Betsy, a good-natured fat man, an ardent collector of engravings, hearing that his wife had visitors, came into the drawing-room before going to his club. Stepping noiselessly over the thick rugs, he went up to Princess Myakaya.

cases.sentence: Эффект, производимый речами княгини Мягкой, всегда был одинаков, и секрет производимого ею эффекта состоял в том, что она говорила хотя и не совсем кстати, как теперь, но ___, имеющие смысл.
cases.explain: «простые вещи» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: The sensation produced by Princess Myakaya’s speeches was always unique, and the secret of the sensation she produced lay in the fact that though she spoke not always appropriately, as now, she said simple things with some sense in them. In the society in which she lived such plain statements produced the effect of the wittiest epigram. Princess Myakaya could never see why it had that effect, but she knew it had, and took advantage of it.

cases.translation: “Anna is quite changed since her stay in Moscow. There’s something strange about her,” said her friend.

cases.sentence: – Типун вам на язык, – сказала вдруг княгиня Мягкая, услыхав эти слова. – Каренина ___.
cases.explain: «прекрасная женщина» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: “Bad luck to your tongue!” said Princess Myakaya suddenly. “Madame Karenina’s a splendid woman. I don’t like her husband, but I like her very much.”

cases.sentence: Он такой ___, – сказала жена посланника. – Муж говорит, что таких государственных людей мало в Европе.
cases.explain: «замечательный человек» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: “Why don’t you like her husband? He’s such a remarkable man,” said the ambassador’s wife. “My husband says there are few statesmen like him in Europe.”

cases.sentence: У меня нет ___.
cases.explain: «другого выхода» — the genitive here marks possession, absence, or quantity.
cases.translation: “Not a bit. I’d no other way out of it. One of the two had to be a fool. And, well, you know one can’t say that of oneself.”

cases.sentence: И, отделав, как следовало, приятельницу Анны, княгиня Мягкая встала и вместе с женой посланника присоединилась к столу, где шел ___ о прусском короле.
cases.explain: «общий разговор» — the subject of the sentence stands in the nominative.
cases.translation: And having duly disposed of Anna’s friend, the Princess Myakaya got up, and together with the ambassador’s wife, joined the group at the table, where the conversation was dealing with the king of Prussia.

cases.sentence: Кажется, в ___, и все с новым удовольствием.
cases.explain: «сотый раз» — after the preposition «в», the accusative marks the direct object of the verb.
cases.translation: “Where do I come from?” he said, in answer to a question from the ambassador’s wife. “Well, there’s no help for it, I must confess. From the opera bouffe. I do believe I’ve seen it a hundred times, and always with fresh enjoyment. It’s exquisite! I know it’s disgraceful, but I go to sleep at the opera, and I sit out the opera bouffe to the last minute, and enjoy it. This evening. …”
